newsitem.title: USA: Trade gap may push Brazil to reform - U.S. experts.
newsitem.headline: Trade gap may push Brazil to reform - U.S. experts.

text.p: The widening of Brazil's trade deficit did not unnerve Wall Street analysts, but did harden their convictions that Brasilia must make progress to mend fiscal imbalances and further privatizations.

U.S. economists said Brazil's record $1.308 billion trade gap for October would pose serious implications if the trend continued, but special factors -- such as higher oil prices -- may have led to a temporary surge last month.

"Such a deficit in Brazil is most likely financeable, as they move toward more long-term direct foreign investment, but they need an improving macroeconomic environment on the fiscal side and on privatization," Paulo Leme, director of emerging market economics at Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc, said.

Analysts said the emerging debt market was acutely sensitive to current account deficits because of Mexico's financial collapse in 1994, but the Brazil problem, estimated at 3.0 percent of GDP this year, was far less severe than the Mexican gap of 8.0 percent of GDP prior to its crisis.

The emerging debt market, which had fixated on the data for weeks, barely blinked on the news. Brazilian "C" bonds BR8D14=RR came off their highs after the release, but still stood 3/8 higher to a 70-7/8 bid in the afternoon.
The market may have priced in the elevated trade number, which was high, but not above the highest forecasts.

"The market would have had a more violent reaction if it had come in over $1.5 billion," said Walter Molano, director of Latin American economic research at SBC Warburg. "The market is going to start settling down as this recedes into history."
Brazilian economists interviewed by Reuters sounded alarmed by the data, but U.S. analysts said they would reserve judgement until they saw more evidence of a trend.
William Romary, Latin American economist at UBS Securities, said the data outpaced his expectations but added that he did not expect any change in Brazil's policy as a result.

"If this trading pattern were to continue then definitely we would be worried, but we think there would be a shift in policy before things got to a worrisome level," Romary said. "They still have plenty of inflows and lots of reserves."
Should reserves begin to deteriorate, then the Brazilians would probaby accelerate the rate of the real depreciation or impose trade restrictions, Romary said.
